extracted.intended_audience: analysts and policy staff in U.S. Federal agencies preparing regulatory analyses for rulemaking and submission to OMB/OIRA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing high-quality, evidence-based regulatory analyses of proposed and final federal regulations, emphasizing benefit-cost analysis (BCA) and related analytic practices to inform policymakers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and quality of regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: This Circular is designed to assist analysts in regulatory agencies by providing guidance on conducting high-quality and evidence-based regulatory analysis and standardizing the way benefits and costs of Federal regulatory actions are measured and reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analysis is a tool to anticipate and evaluate likely consequences of regulatory actions, inform policymakers and the public, and clarify likely effects of a regulation under consideration. Conducting high-quality analysis requires competent professional judgment; analyses should aim for specificity and reconsider prior less-specific approaches when greater specificity is now practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) as primary tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit-cost analysis is the primary analytical tool used for regulatory analysis; both benefits and costs should be expressed in monetary units to the extent feasible so alternatives can be evaluated using a common measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetized net benefits (monetized benefits minus monetized costs) indicate which analyzed alternative generates the largest welfare improvement, but when important effects cannot be monetized, monetized net benefits are incomplete. Do not use benefit-cost ratios as an indicator of net benefits; exercise professional judgment when unquantified factors are important and consider threshold analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include quantified and non-monetized effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When benefits or costs cannot be expressed in monetary units, measure in physical or other quantitative units if possible; otherwise describe qualitatively using the best available methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be as specific as possible in presenting non-monetized/unquantified effects; categorize or rank non-monetized/unquantified effects by importance where feasible, and explain how such factors might change the ranking of alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA)
rubrics_metrics.description: CEA can be used to compare options that achieve the most effective use of resources when monetization is not possible; it compares cost per unit of a common effectiveness measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all important societal costs in the numerator (net costs = gross costs minus cost savings), prefer final outcomes as effectiveness measures, avoid double-counting between numerator and denominator, explain choice of effectiveness measure, present incremental CEA (not just average ratios), eliminate dominated alternatives, and recognize CEA's limits when multiple disparate outcomes exist (in which case BCA is preferred if monetization is possible). OMB does not require CEA and encourages BCA when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and evaluate the need for regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis must identify and evaluate the potential needs for Federal regulatory action—i.e., whether a problem exists and the role regulation could play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key elements of analysis include identifying the need for action, defining the baseline, identifying alternatives, gathering evidence, estimating or describing benefits and costs of each alternative, and summarizing the analysis. Iteration and refinement are expected as analysis proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define an analytic baseline (no-action baseline preferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits and costs of a regulation are generally measured against a no-action baseline—an analytically reasonable forecast of the world absent the regulatory action, grounded in sound theories and empirical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The baseline should reflect market evolution, expected regulatory changes, external factors, compliance with other regulations, and the scale of affected entities. Use a with-statute baseline only in rare cases where the statute is self-implementing for most elements, and consult OMB early if planning to use a with-statute baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial scope: focus on U.S. citizens and residents (with appropriate inclusion of foreign effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary analyses should focus on effects experienced by U.S. citizens and residents, but when feasible/appropriate, include important effects regardless of domestic or foreign source; supplementary analyses of foreign effects are encouraged when primary analysis focuses domestically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include foreign effects when they affect U.S. citizens/residents via markets or non-market channels, when global effects are required by law/policy, or when foreign effects are useful proxies for U.S. effects or national interests. Be consistent in including countervailing foreign effects (e.g., include benefits and corresponding compliance costs). Transparently report decisions and data limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope: choose time horizon to capture all important effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytic time frame should include a period before and after the compliance date long enough to encompass all important benefits and costs likely to result from the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the stream of estimates in the year the regulation begins to have effects. The end point should be far enough in the future to capture changes that could alter net benefit signs or rankings. Do not artificially shorten horizons to avoid uncertain long-term effects; consult sections on uncertainty and hard-to-quantify effects as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about methods, data, and analytical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should be transparent about key methods, data, modeling choices, inclusion/exclusion decisions, and uncertainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear explanations for choices (e.g., inclusion of noncitizens residing abroad), describe data limitations, and make supporting materials available in regulatory dockets and on agency websites. Documentation should enable reviewers to understand and reproduce results where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder consultation and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: When feasible and appropriate, agencies should seek opinions of those affected by the regulation and those with special knowledge, early in the analytical process and not only at the final stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation can help characterize dignity, equity, or fairness effects and ensure relevant issues and data are included. Be mindful of the Paperwork Reduction Act when consultations involve information collections that meet its threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of uncertainty and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide central estimates and distributions where possible; when only bounds are provided, use 5 and 95 percent confidence bounds if appropriate and construct distributions of plausible outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage development of estimates that capture distribution of plausible outcomes. Use threshold analyses when unquantified factors might change alternative rankings. Clearly state assumptions behind risk assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounting and presentation of annualized estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Report undiscounted streams of benefits, costs, and net benefits for each year and generally present annualized benefits and costs consistent with Discount Rates guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annualized streams should start in the year regulation begins to have effects. Report monetized effects in constant dollars (state dollar year) and convert using appropriate price deflators (e.g., BEA GDP deflator or PCE index). Use standard spreadsheet functions for annualization and document discount rates used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect the precision in the analysis; implied rounding should match stated precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, reporting $220 million implies rounding to nearest $10 million (precision +/- $5 million). Choose digit/reporting conventions consistent with analytical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout listing estimates, agencies should avoid double-counting effects when more than one way exists to express the same change in social welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay special attention when expressing effects across multiple categories (e.g., monetized benefits, transfers, and distributional impacts) to not count the same welfare change more than once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report transfers separately from societal benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should identify transfers (including federal budgetary transfers) separately and report who bears transfer gains and losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include annualized monetized transfers in the accounting statement and identify bearers of transfer gains and losses to distinguish transfers from net effects on social welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement and standardized presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: For each regulation significant under Executive Order 12866, include an accounting statement (preferably in executive summary) with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates categorized as monetized, quantified-but-not-monetized, and unquantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide separate tables for annual undiscounted streams and annualized amounts; include fields for primary/low/high estimates, dollar year, discount rate, time horizon, and notes on risk assumptions and sources. Include sections reporting effects on state/local/Tribal governments, small businesses, wages, and growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Report benefit and cost estimates within three categories: monetized; quantified, but not monetized; and unquantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Agencies should, where feasible, rank or categorize non-monetized effects by their importance and explain which effects are likely to be significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all important costs to society when measuring costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring costs (including for CEA), include all important costs to society, whether public or private, and reflect cost savings where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define numerator in cost-effectiveness as net costs (gross compliance costs minus cost savings). Avoid double-counting (e.g., don't subtract monetary values used in denominators) and be explicit about how capital effects are treated across estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and construction of effectiveness measures in CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness measures should preferably be final outcomes (e.g., injuries reduced, lives saved) rather than intermediate outputs; measures should capture quality differences where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain choice of measure, prefer indices that weight quality (e.g., wetland quality), avoid simplified aggregated units that hide heterogeneity across outcomes, and acknowledge limits when multiple beneficial outcomes exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with alternatives and dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing a range of alternatives, determine incremental cost-effectiveness and identify/eliminate options that are strongly or weakly dominated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether alternatives are mutually exclusive or combinable, select reasonable subsets for detailed analysis when many options exist, and consider which alternatives are favored under different regulatory budget constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of noncitizens residing abroad and global effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to include effects on noncitizens residing abroad in primary analysis; when primary analysis focuses domestically, supplementary analyses of foreign effects may inform policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include foreign effects in primary analysis when they are useful proxies, capture U.S. national interests, support international cooperation, or are required by law. Be consistent (if including benefits experienced abroad, include corresponding costs) and transparent about inclusion/exclusion and data uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for compliance and take-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic baseline and regulatory impact estimates should reflect expected degree of compliance with regulations and take-up of programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate realistic assumptions about compliance when establishing baseline and estimating incremental effects; consult section 'Accounting for Compliance and Take-up' for methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of market evolution, technology, and other trends in baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Baselines should reflect anticipated future changes (technological advances, demographic shifts, economic trends, climate change) that will affect regulatory impacts absent the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust baseline for future government programs and policy changes that are reasonably certain to occur; consider consulting other agencies for data/models on such trends and present supplementary baselines where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use threshold analysis for important unquantified factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When unquantified benefits or costs might change the ranking of alternatives, conduct threshold analyses to show how large such effects would need to be to alter conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why unquantified factors are important and present threshold or sensitivity analyses to aid decisionmakers in understanding potential significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate reliance on benefit-cost or cost-effectiveness ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit-cost ratios and average cost-effectiveness ratios alone are not reliable indicators of which alternative maximizes net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use net benefit differences and incremental comparisons rather than ratios to rank alternatives; clarify how negative WTP/WTA valuations are treated and why ratios can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality, objectivity, transparency, and reproducibility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses and underlying data must meet agency and OMB Information Quality Act performance goals; OMB defines minimum quality standards for regulatory analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure data and analysis conform to agency data quality guidelines, document sources and methods, and make materials available in dockets. Consult agency CIO or OMB Statistical and Science Policy Branch for assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements (statutory and executive order-driven)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and satisfy specialized analytic requirements imposed by statutes and Executive Orders, such as Regulatory Flexibility Act, Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, NEPA, EO 14096 (environmental justice), EO 13045 (children's health/safety), and EO 13211 (energy effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare required separate analyses (e.g., RFA, written statement under Unfunded Mandates) when thresholds/conditions apply; consult relevant statutory guidance and agency offices (e.g., Chief Counsel for Advocacy, CIO) and include required documentation with rulemaking. Where analyses overlap, use consistent methods and note transfers vs. societal impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting effects on state, local, Tribal governments, small businesses, wages, and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits and costs experienced by State, local, and Tribal governments, and, to the extent feasible, effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification may be required by statutes like Unfunded Mandates Reform Act and Regulatory Flexibility Act. Report such effects in dedicated accounting-statement fields and provide notes explaining estimation methods and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make analysis available and docket materials accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish regulatory analyses and supporting documents (notices, scientific findings, regulatory impact analyses) timely and make them available in regulatory dockets and agency websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simultaneous dissemination with proposed/final rule is encouraged; because web links can break, include materials in Regulations.gov dockets. For proposed rules, include opportunity for public comment on supporting scientific/technical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether federal regulation is the best approach and consider trade effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Show whether regulation at the federal level is the appropriate way to solve the problem and, when appropriate, evaluate effects on international trade (e.g., import/export volumes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider non-regulatory approaches and state/local options, and analyze trade impacts where required. Report changes in trade volumes as metrics but not as direct welfare measures and explain their relevance.
